sections.raw_text: Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any woman or abets such act with the intention of disrobing or compelling her to be naked, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than three years but which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: intent to disrobe or compel nakedness

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 76 specifically targets assault, criminal force, or abetment thereof done with the intention of disrobing a woman or compelling her to be naked — a more severe punishment band (minimum three years, up to seven years, plus fine) than the general modesty-outraging offence in Section 74, reflecting the heightened gravity of this specific form of degradation.
essential_elements: Assault or use of criminal force against a woman, or abetment of such act.
Intention of disrobing her or compelling her to be naked.
Punishment: imprisonment of either description, minimum three years, up to seven years, plus fine.
breakdown.how_to_read: Note that abetment of this specific act is itself directly criminalised within Section 76's own text, rather than being left to the general Chapter IV abetment-punishment scheme.

sections.title: Voyeurism
sections.raw_text: Whoever watches, or captures the image of a woman engaging in a private act in circumstances where she would usually have the expectation of not being observed either by the perpetrator or by any other person at the behest of the perpetrator or disseminates such image shall be punished on first conviction with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than one year, but which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine, and be punished on a second or subsequent conviction, with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than three years, but which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. Explanation 1.—For the purposes of this section, “private act” includes an act of watching carried out in a place which, in the circumstances, would reasonably be expected to provide privacy and where the victim's genitals, posterior or breasts are exposed or covered only in underwear; or the victim is using a lavatory; or the victim is doing a sexual act that is not of a kind ordinarily done in public. Explanation 2.—Where the victim consents to the capture of the images or any act, but not to their dissemination to third persons and where such image or act is disseminated, such dissemination shall be considered an offence under this section.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 77 criminalises watching or image-capturing a woman engaged in a 'private act' in circumstances where she reasonably expected not to be observed, as well as disseminating such images, with an escalating two-tier punishment scheme (one-to-three years on first conviction, three-to-seven years on repeat conviction, plus fine in either case). Explanation 1 defines 'private act' concretely (exposed genitals/posterior/breasts, lavatory use, or non-public sexual acts), and Explanation 2 confirms that consenting to image capture does not extend to consenting to its dissemination — unauthorised dissemination remains independently punishable.
essential_elements: Watching, capturing the image of, or disseminating an image of, a woman engaging in a 'private act' as defined in Explanation 1.
The circumstances were ones in which she would usually expect not to be observed.
Punishment escalates from first conviction (one to three years plus fine) to second/subsequent conviction (three to seven years plus fine).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Consent to the capture of images or the act itself does not extend to consent for their dissemination to third persons — dissemination beyond that consent remains an offence under Explanation 2.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 77 is squarely aimed at both the act of covert observation/recording and its unauthorised circulation — the two Explanations are essential to correctly scoping both halves of the offence.

sections.title: Stalking
sections.raw_text: (1) Any man who— (i) follows a woman and contacts, or attempts to contact such woman to foster personal interaction repeatedly despite a clear indication of disinterest by such woman; or (ii) monitors the use by a woman of the internet, e-mail or any other form of electronic communication, commits the offence of stalking: Provided that such conduct shall not amount to stalking if the man who pursued it proves that— (i) it was pursued for the purpose of preventing or detecting crime and the man accused of stalking had been entrusted with the responsibility of prevention and detection of crime by the State; or (ii) it was pursued under any law or to comply with any condition or requirement imposed by any person under any law; or (iii) in the particular circumstances such conduct was reasonable and justified. (2) Whoever commits the offence of stalking shall be punished on first conviction with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine; and be punished on a second or subsequent conviction, with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 78 defines stalking through two alternative forms of conduct — persistent physical pursuit/contact attempts despite a clear indication of disinterest, or monitoring a woman's internet/email/electronic-communication use — with an escalating punishment scheme (up to three years on first conviction, up to five years on repeat conviction, plus fine in both cases). The proviso supplies three statutory defences the accused bears the burden of proving: lawful crime-prevention duty entrusted by the State, conduct pursued under or to comply with a legal requirement, or conduct that was otherwise reasonable and justified in the circumstances.
essential_elements: One of two forms of conduct: repeated contact-fostering pursuit despite clear disinterest, or monitoring the woman's electronic communications.
The offender is a man (gender-specific as to the offender, as drafted).
Punishment escalates from first conviction (up to three years plus fine) to second/subsequent conviction (up to five years plus fine).
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso supplies three defences, which the accused must prove: lawful State-entrusted crime prevention/detection duty; conduct pursued under or to comply with legal requirements; or conduct that was reasonable and justified in the particular circumstances.
breakdown.how_to_read: The proviso's three defences function as a reverse-onus scheme — once the conduct falls within clause (i) or (ii) of sub-section (1), the accused must affirmatively prove one of the statutory defences, rather than the prosecution having to negate them.

sections.title: Word, gesture or act intended to insult modesty of a woman
sections.raw_text: Whoever, intending to insult the modesty of any woman, utters any words, makes any sound or gesture, or exhibits any object in any form, intending that such word or sound shall be heard, or that such gesture or object shall be seen, by such woman, or intrudes upon the privacy of such woman, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also with fine.
key_terms: insult to the modesty of a woman by word, sound, gesture or object

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 79 is the Sanhita's catch-all provision for verbal, auditory, gestural, or visual insults to a woman's modesty — including privacy intrusion — punishable with up to three years' simple imprisonment and mandatory fine, where the conduct does not rise to the level of the more specific offences (assault/criminal force, harassment, disrobing, voyeurism, stalking) covered elsewhere in this sub-chapter.
essential_elements: Intention to insult the modesty of a woman.
Conduct taking the form of uttered words, sound, gesture, or exhibited object, intended to be heard or seen by her — or intrusion upon her privacy.
Punishment: simple imprisonment up to three years, and fine (both mandatory, not alternative).
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 79 closes the 'Of sexual offences'/'Of criminal force and assault against woman' run of sections as the residual, lower-threshold offence for modesty-insulting conduct that does not fit the more specific, more severely punished provisions preceding it.

sections.title: Dowry death
sections.raw_text: (1) Where the death of a woman is caused by any burns or bodily injury or occurs otherwise than under normal circumstances within seven years of her marriage and it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any relative of her husband for, or in connection with, any demand for dowry, such death shall be called “dowry death”, and such husband or relative shall be deemed to have caused her death. Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-section, “dowry” shall have the same meaning as in section 2 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961. (2) Whoever commits dowry death shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than seven years but which may extend to imprisonment for life.
key_terms: soon before death cruelty or harassment for dowry

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 80 defines 'dowry death' as an unnatural death (by burns, bodily injury, or otherwise abnormal circumstances) of a married woman within seven years of marriage, where she was shown to have been subjected to dowry-related cruelty or harassment by her husband or his relatives 'soon before' her death — on proof of these elements, the husband or relative is deemed to have caused the death, and faces seven years to life imprisonment.
essential_elements: Death of a woman caused by burns, bodily injury, or occurring otherwise than under normal circumstances.
The death occurs within seven years of her marriage.
It is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or his relative, for or in connection with a dowry demand.
On proof of these elements, the husband or relative concerned is deemed to have caused the death.
breakdown.how_to_read: The 'deeming' mechanism in sub-section (1) is a significant evidentiary tool — the prosecution need not independently prove causation of death in the ordinary sense once the three statutory preconditions (unnatural death within seven years, soon-before cruelty/harassment, dowry connection) are established.

sections.title: Cohabitation caused by man deceitfully inducing belief of lawful marriage
sections.raw_text: Every man who by deceit causes any woman who is not lawfully married to him to believe that she is lawfully married to him and to cohabit or have sexual intercourse with him in that belief, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: deceitful inducement of belief in lawful marriage

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 81 criminalises deceitfully causing a woman to believe she is lawfully married to a man when she is not, and thereby inducing her to cohabit or have sexual intercourse with him under that false belief — punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine.
essential_elements: The accused is a man who deceitfully causes a woman (not lawfully married to him) to believe she is lawfully married to him.
In that false belief, she cohabits or has sexual intercourse with him.
Punishment: imprisonment of either description up to ten years, plus fine.
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish Section 81 (deceit about the existence of a marriage itself) from Section 69 (deceit or false promise to marry more generally) and Section 83 (a fraudulent marriage ceremony) — all three address different forms of marriage-related deception.

sections.title: Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife
sections.raw_text: (1) Whoever, having a husband or wife living, marries in any case in which such marriage is void by reason of its taking place during the life of such husband or wife, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. Exception.—This sub-section does not extend to any person whose marriage with such husband or wife has been declared void by a Court of competent jurisdiction, nor to any person who contracts a marriage during the life of a former husband or wife, if such husband or wife, at the time of the subsequent marriage, shall have been continually absent from such person for the space of seven years, and shall not have been heard of by such person as being alive within that time provided the person contracting such subsequent marriage shall, before such marriage takes place, inform the person with whom such marriage is contracted of the real state of facts so far as the same are within his or her knowledge. (2) Whoever commits the offence under sub-section (1) having concealed from the person with whom the subsequent marriage is contracted, the fact of the former marriage, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 82 criminalises bigamy — contracting a second, legally void marriage while a spouse from an earlier marriage is still living — punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine. The Exception excuses a prior marriage already declared void by a competent court, and the well-known seven-year continuous-absence-and-unheard-of scenario, provided the new spouse is truthfully informed of the facts beforehand. Sub-section (2) raises punishment to up to ten years where the offender concealed the earlier marriage from the new spouse.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1): the accused, having a living spouse, contracts a further marriage void by reason of that earlier marriage.

The Exception removes liability where the prior marriage was judicially declared void, or where the earlier spouse had been continually absent and unheard-of as alive for seven years, with full disclosure to the new spouse.
Sub-section (2): punishment rises to up to ten years where the offender concealed the fact of the earlier marriage from the person with whom the subsequent marriage is contracted.
exceptions_and_qualifications: A prior marriage already declared void by a court of competent jurisdiction is outside the offence.
The seven-years'-continuous-absence-and-unheard-of exception, conditioned on full disclosure to the new spouse before the subsequent marriage.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read sub-sections (1) and (2) as base offence and aggravated (concealment) variant of the same underlying bigamy wrong — concealment from the new spouse is what moves the case from the seven-year to the ten-year maximum.

sections.title: Marriage ceremony fraudulently gone through without lawful marriage
sections.raw_text: Whoever, dishonestly or with a fraudulent intention, goes through the ceremony of being married, knowing that he is not thereby lawfully married, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 83 criminalises dishonestly or fraudulently going through a marriage ceremony while knowing that no lawful marriage results from it — punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine.
essential_elements: The accused goes through a marriage ceremony dishonestly or with fraudulent intention.
The accused knows that he is not thereby lawfully married.
Punishment: imprisonment of either description up to seven years, plus fine.
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish this from Section 82 (bigamy, a second marriage void because of a living spouse) — Section 83 covers the broader scenario of any fraudulent sham ceremony known by the accused to create no valid marriage at all, for whatever reason.

sections.title: Enticing or taking away or detaining with criminal intent a married woman
sections.raw_text: Whoever takes or entices away any woman who is and whom he knows or has reason to believe to be the wife of any other man, with intent that she may have illicit intercourse with any person, or conceals or detains with that intent any such woman, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: concealment or detention of a married woman

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 84 criminalises taking, enticing away, concealing, or detaining a woman known (or reasonably believed) to be another man's wife, done with intent that she may have illicit intercourse with any person — punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
essential_elements: The accused takes, entices away, conceals, or detains a woman.
The accused knows or has reason to believe she is the wife of another man.
The act is done with intent that she may have illicit intercourse with any person.
Punishment: imprisonment of either description up to two years, or fine, or both.
breakdown.how_to_read: This provision protects the marital relationship itself against third-party interference, distinct from the offences against the woman's own bodily autonomy found elsewhere in this chapter.

sections.title: Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty
sections.raw_text: Whoever, being the husband or the relative of the husband of a woman, subjects such woman to cruelty shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: cruelty by husband or his relative

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 85 criminalises cruelty inflicted on a woman by her husband or a relative of her husband, punishable with up to three years' imprisonment plus fine. 'Cruelty' is itself defined immediately after, in Section 86.
essential_elements: The accused is the husband of the woman, or a relative of her husband.
The accused subjects her to cruelty as defined in Section 86.
Punishment: imprisonment up to three years, plus fine.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 85 must always be read together with Section 86's definition of 'cruelty' — the two sections form a single operative unit, continuing the BNS's drafting convention (seen earlier with abetment and rape) of a definitional section immediately following the offence-creating one.

sections.title: Cruelty defined
sections.raw_text: For the purposes of section 85, “cruelty” means— (a) any wilful conduct which is of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health (whether mental or physical) of the woman; or (b) harassment of the woman where such harassment is with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any property or valuable security or is on account of failure by her or any person related to her to meet such demand.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 86 defines 'cruelty' for purposes of Section 85 through two limbs: wilful conduct likely to drive the woman to suicide or cause grave injury/danger to her life, limb, or mental or physical health (clause (a)); or harassment aimed at coercing her or her relatives to meet an unlawful property/valuable-security demand, or inflicted on account of a failure to meet such a demand (clause (b), closely linked to the dowry-harassment pattern addressed also in Section 80).
essential_elements: Clause (a): wilful conduct likely to drive the woman to suicide, or to cause grave injury or danger to her life, limb, or health (mental or physical).
Clause (b): harassment aimed at coercing an unlawful property/valuable-security demand from her or her relatives, or inflicted because such a demand was not met.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 86's clause (b) definition deliberately overlaps with the dowry-harassment language of Section 80 — the same underlying harassment pattern can found both a Section 85 cruelty prosecution and, where death results, a Section 80 dowry-death prosecution.

sections.title: Kidnapping, abducting or inducing woman to compel her marriage, etc.
sections.raw_text: Whoever kidnaps or abducts any woman with intent that she may be compelled, or knowing it to be likely that she will be compelled, to marry any person against her will, or in order that she may be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse, or knowing it to be likely that she will be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine; and whoever, by means of criminal intimidation as defined in this Sanhita or of abuse of authority or any other method of compulsion, induces any woman to go from any place with intent that she may be, or knowing that it is likely that she will be, forced or seduced to illicit intercourse with another person shall also be punishable as aforesaid.
key_terms: kidnapping or abducting a woman to compel marriage
inducement by criminal intimidation or abuse of authority

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 87 criminalises kidnapping or abducting a woman with intent (or knowledge of likelihood) that she be compelled into marriage against her will or forced/seduced into illicit intercourse, and separately criminalises inducing a woman to leave a place by criminal intimidation, abuse of authority, or other compulsion, with the same forced-marriage or illicit-intercourse intent or knowledge — both limbs punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine.
essential_elements: First limb: kidnapping or abducting a woman, with intent or knowledge of likelihood that she be compelled to marry against her will, or forced/seduced into illicit intercourse.
Second limb: inducing a woman to leave any place by criminal intimidation, abuse of authority, or other compulsion, with the same forced-marriage/illicit-intercourse intent or knowledge.
Punishment (either limb): imprisonment of either description up to ten years, plus fine.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 87 should be read together with the general kidnapping/abduction provisions found later in the Sanhita's chapter on offences affecting the human body — this section supplies a specific, aggravated purpose-based variant aimed at forced marriage and illicit intercourse.

sections.title: Causing miscarriage
sections.raw_text: Whoever voluntarily causes a woman with child to miscarry, shall, if such miscarriage be not caused in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the woman, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both; and, if the woman be quick with child, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. Explanation.—A woman who causes herself to miscarry, is within the meaning of this section.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 88 criminalises voluntarily causing a pregnant woman to miscarry, unless done in good faith to save her life — punishable with up to three years' imprisonment or fine or both, rising to up to seven years plus fine if the woman was 'quick with child' (i.e. at a more advanced stage of pregnancy where foetal movement is perceptible). The Explanation confirms that a woman who causes her own miscarriage is herself within the offence's scope.
essential_elements: Voluntarily causing a woman with child to miscarry.
Not done in good faith to save the woman's life.
Base punishment: up to three years' imprisonment or fine or both; enhanced to up to seven years plus fine if the woman was quick with child.
The offence applies equally to a woman who causes her own miscarriage (Explanation).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Miscarriage caused in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the woman is excluded from the offence.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 88 is the base miscarriage offence; Sections 89-90 build on it for the non-consensual and death-resulting aggravations respectively.

sections.title: Causing miscarriage without woman's consent
sections.raw_text: Whoever commits the offence under section 88 without the consent of the woman, whether the woman is quick with child or not, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 89 significantly escalates punishment where the Section 88 miscarriage offence is committed without the woman's consent at all (regardless of whether she was quick with child): life imprisonment, or up to ten years' imprisonment of either description, plus fine.
essential_elements: The underlying conduct is an offence under Section 88.
It is committed without the woman's consent.
Punishment: life imprisonment, or imprisonment of either description up to ten years, plus fine — this applies whether or not the woman was quick with child.
breakdown.how_to_read: Consent is the pivotal aggravating factor distinguishing Section 89 from Section 88 — its absence roughly doubles the available maximum sentence and adds life imprisonment as an option.

sections.title: Death caused by act done with intent to cause miscarriage
sections.raw_text: (1) Whoever, with intent to cause the miscarriage of a woman with child, does any act which causes the death of such woman, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. (2) Where the act referred to in sub-section (1) is done without the consent of the woman, shall be punishable either with imprisonment for life, or with the punishment specified in said sub-section. Explanation.—It is not essential to this offence that the offender should know that the act is likely to cause death.
key_terms: death resulting from an act intended to cause miscarriage

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 90 punishes causing a pregnant woman's death through an act done with intent to cause her miscarriage, even without any knowledge that death was a likely consequence — up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine, escalating to a possible life imprisonment where the act was done without the woman's consent.
essential_elements: An act done with intent to cause the miscarriage of a woman with child.
That act causes the woman's death.
Base punishment: imprisonment of either description up to ten years, plus fine.
Enhanced to life imprisonment (or the base punishment) where the act was done without the woman's consent.
Knowledge that the act was likely to cause death is not an essential ingredient (Explanation).
breakdown.how_to_read: The Explanation is important: unlike many homicide-adjacent offences, Section 90 does not require the offender to have foreseen death as a likely outcome — the mere causal link between the miscarriage-intended act and the resulting death suffices.

sections.title: Act done with intent to prevent child being born alive or to cause it to die after birth
sections.raw_text: Whoever before the birth of any child does any act with the intention of thereby preventing that child from being born alive or causing it to die after its birth, and does by such act prevent that child from being born alive, or causes it to die after its birth, shall, if such act be not caused in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the mother, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: preventing live birth or causing death after birth

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 91 criminalises a pre-birth act done with the intention of preventing a child from being born alive, or of causing its death after birth, where that intended result actually occurs — punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment, fine, or both, unless done in good faith to save the mother's life.
essential_elements: An act is done before the birth of a child, with intention of preventing live birth or causing death after birth.
The act actually results in the child not being born alive, or dying after birth.
Not done in good faith to save the mother's life.
Punishment: imprisonment of either description up to ten years, or fine, or both.
exceptions_and_qualifications: An act done in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the mother is excluded from the offence.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 91 is distinct from Section 88's miscarriage offence — it covers acts aimed at a later stage, specifically preventing live birth or causing post-birth death, rather than inducing miscarriage itself.

sections.title: Causing death of quick unborn child by act amounting to culpable homicide
sections.raw_text: Whoever does any act under such circumstances, that if he thereby caused death he would be guilty of culpable homicide, and does by such act cause the death of a quick unborn child, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. Illustration.—A, knowing that he is likely to cause the death of a pregnant woman, does an act which, if it caused the death of the woman, would amount to culpable homicide. The woman is injured, but does not die; but the death of an unborn quick child with which she is pregnant is thereby caused. A is guilty of the offence defined in this section.
key_terms: culpable-homicide-equivalent act causing death of a quick unborn child

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 92 bridges the general culpable-homicide standard (Section 100) with harm to an unborn child: where an act is done under circumstances such that, had it caused the mother's death, would amount to culpable homicide, and the act instead causes the death of a quick unborn child, the offender is punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine — illustrated by a case where the mother survives injured but the unborn quick child dies.
essential_elements: An act done under circumstances that, had death of the mother resulted, would amount to culpable homicide.
The act instead causes the death of a quick unborn child.
Punishment: imprisonment of either description up to ten years, plus fine.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 92 should be read against the backdrop of Section 100's culpable-homicide definition and its Explanation 3 (death of a child in the womb is not homicide, but death of a living child partly brought forth may be) — Section 92 is the Sanhita's specific bridge for the quick-unborn-child scenario that falls outside ordinary culpable homicide.

sections.title: Exposure and abandonment of child under twelve years of age by parent or person having care of it
sections.raw_text: Whoever being the father or mother of a child under the age of twelve years, or having the care of such child, shall expose or leave such child in any place with the intention of wholly abandoning such child, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both. Explanation.—This section is not intended to prevent the trial of the offender for murder or culpable homicide, as the case may be, if the child die in consequence of the exposure.
key_terms: exposure and abandonment of a child under twelve

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 93 criminalises a parent's or caregiver's exposure or abandonment of a child under twelve years of age with intention of wholly abandoning the child, punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment, fine, or both. The Explanation preserves the possibility of a separate murder or culpable homicide prosecution if the child actually dies as a result of the exposure.
essential_elements: The accused is the father, mother, or a person having care of a child under twelve years of age.
The accused exposes or leaves the child in any place with the intention of wholly abandoning it.
Punishment: imprisonment of either description up to seven years, or fine, or both.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This section does not bar a separate trial for murder or culpable homicide if the child dies in consequence of the exposure (Explanation).
breakdown.how_to_read: This section opens the 'Of offences against child' sub-chapter — note the Explanation's careful preservation of homicide liability where the abandonment proves fatal, so Section 93 is not read as capping liability at seven years in a death case.

sections.title: Concealment of birth by secret disposal of dead body
sections.raw_text: Whoever, by secretly burying or otherwise disposing of the dead body of a child whether such child die before or after or during its birth, intentionally conceals or endeavours to conceal the birth of such child, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
key_terms: concealment of birth by secret disposal of a dead body

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 94 criminalises secretly burying or otherwise disposing of a dead child's body with intention to conceal the fact of that child's birth — regardless of whether the child died before, during, or after birth — punishable with up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both.
essential_elements: Secret burial or other disposal of the dead body of a child (irrespective of whether the child died before, during, or after birth).
Intentional concealment, or an endeavour to conceal, the birth of the child.
Punishment: imprisonment of either description up to two years, or fine, or both.
breakdown.how_to_read: The offence targets the act of concealment itself, independent of (and not a substitute for) any separate liability that might arise from how the child actually died.

sections.title: Hiring, employing or engaging a child to commit an offence
sections.raw_text: Whoever hires, employs or engages any child to commit an offence shall be punished with imprisonment of either description which shall not be less than three years but which may extend to ten years, and with fine; and if the offence be committed shall also be punished with the punishment provided for that offence as if the offence has been committed by such person himself. Explanation.—Hiring, employing, engaging or using a child for sexual exploitation or pornography is covered within the meaning of this section.
key_terms: hiring or engaging a child to commit an offence
cumulative liability for the resulting offence

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 95 criminalises hiring, employing, or engaging a child to commit an offence, with a mandatory minimum of three years' imprisonment up to ten years, plus fine — and, crucially, if the offence the child was engaged to commit is actually carried out, the hirer/employer also separately incurs the full punishment for that offence as though they had committed it personally. The Explanation confirms this covers using a child for sexual exploitation or pornography.
essential_elements: Hiring, employing, or engaging a child to commit an offence.
Base punishment: imprisonment of either description, minimum three years, up to ten years, plus fine.
If the offence is actually committed, the hirer/employer is additionally liable to the punishment prescribed for that offence, as if they had committed it themselves.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 95's Explanation extending coverage to sexual exploitation and pornography links this provision to the broader child-protection scheme spanning the rest of this sub-chapter (Sections 96, 98, 99).

sections.title: Procuration of child
sections.raw_text: Whoever, by any means whatsoever, induces any child to go from any place or to do any act with intent that such child may be, or knowing that it is likely that such child will be, forced or seduced to illicit intercourse with another person shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: procuration of a child for illicit intercourse

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 96 criminalises inducing a child, by any means, to leave a place or do an act, with intent or knowledge of likelihood that the child will be forced or seduced into illicit intercourse with another person — punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine. This mirrors Section 87's adult-woman equivalent, applied here to children.
essential_elements: Inducement of a child, by any means, to go from a place or do an act.
Intent or knowledge of likelihood that the child will be forced or seduced into illicit intercourse with another person.
Punishment: imprisonment up to ten years, plus fine.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 96 for children parallels Section 87's second limb for adult women — both target third-party procurement/inducement toward illicit intercourse, with the child-specific version carrying no lower bound on the inducement method ('by any means whatsoever').

sections.title: Kidnapping or abducting child under ten years of age with intent to steal from its person
sections.raw_text: Whoever kidnaps or abducts any child under the age of ten years with the intention of taking dishonestly any movable property from the person of such child, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
key_terms: kidnapping a child under ten to steal from its person

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 97 criminalises kidnapping or abducting a child under ten years of age with the specific intention of dishonestly taking movable property from the child's person — punishable with up to seven years' imprisonment plus fine. This is a property-motivated kidnapping offence distinct from the sexual/marriage-motivated kidnapping provisions elsewhere in this chapter.
essential_elements: Kidnapping or abducting a child under the age of ten years.
Done with the intention of dishonestly taking movable property from the child's person.
Punishment: imprisonment of either description up to seven years, plus fine.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 97 is narrowly purpose-specific — its gist is the dishonest property-taking intent, making it conceptually closer to theft-via-kidnapping than to the chapter's sexual-offence provisions.

sections.title: Selling child for purposes of prostitution, etc.
sections.raw_text: Whoever sells, lets to hire, or otherwise disposes of any child with intent that such child shall at any age be employed or used for the purpose of prostitution or illicit intercourse with any person or for any unlawful and immoral purpose, or knowing it to be likely that such child will at any age be employed or used for any such purpose, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. Explanation 1.—When a female under the age of eighteen years is sold, let for hire, or otherwise disposed of to a prostitute or to any person who keeps or manages a brothel, the person so disposing of such female shall, until the contrary is proved, be presumed to have disposed of her with the intent that she shall be used for the purpose of prostitution. Explanation 2.—For the purposes of this section “illicit intercourse” means sexual intercourse between persons not united by marriage or by any union or tie which, though not amounting to a marriage, is recognised by the personal law or custom of the community to which they belong or, where they belong to different communities, of both such communities, as constituting between them a quasi-marital relation.
key_terms: selling a child for prostitution or illicit purposes

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 98 criminalises selling, letting to hire, or otherwise disposing of a child with intent (or knowledge of likelihood) that the child be used, at any age, for prostitution, illicit intercourse, or any unlawful and immoral purpose — punishable with up to ten years' imprisonment plus fine. Explanation 1 creates a reverse statutory presumption: disposing of a female under eighteen to a prostitute or brothel-keeper/manager is presumed (until rebutted) to be done with prostitution intent. Explanation 2 defines 'illicit intercourse' broadly to include sexual unions outside marriage that nonetheless lack even quasi-marital community recognition.
essential_elements: Selling, letting to hire, or otherwise disposing of a child.
Intent, or knowledge of likelihood, that the child will at any age be employed or used for prostitution, illicit intercourse, or any unlawful and immoral purpose.
Punishment: imprisonment of either description up to ten years, plus fine.
Explanation 1's presumption shifts the evidentiary burden onto the accused where the child is a female under eighteen disposed of to a prostitute or brothel-keeper/manager.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 98's reverse presumption in Explanation 1 is a significant prosecutorial tool — once the basic facts (female under eighteen, disposal to a prostitute/brothel-keeper) are shown, the burden shifts to the accused to disprove prostitution intent.

sections.title: Buying child for purposes of prostitution, etc.
sections.raw_text: Whoever buys, hires or otherwise obtains possession of any child with intent that such child shall at any age be employed or used for the purpose of prostitution or illicit intercourse with any person or for any unlawful and immoral purpose, or knowing it to be likely that such child will at any age be employed or used for any such purpose, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than seven years but which may extend to fourteen years, and shall also be liable to fine. Explanation 1.—Any prostitute or any person keeping or managing a brothel, who buys, hires or otherwise obtains possession of a female under the age of eighteen years shall, until the contrary is proved, be presumed to have obtained possession of such female with the intent that she shall be used for the purpose of prostitution. Explanation 2.—“Illicit intercourse” has the same meaning as in section 98.
key_terms: buying a child for prostitution or illicit purposes

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 99 is the demand-side mirror of Section 98: buying, hiring, or otherwise obtaining possession of a child with the same prostitution/illicit-intercourse/unlawful-and-immoral-purpose intent or knowledge, punishable with a mandatory minimum of seven years' imprisonment up to fourteen years, plus fine — a notably higher minimum and maximum than the supply-side Section 98 offence. Explanation 1 mirrors Section 98's reverse presumption, applied here to a prostitute or brothel-keeper/manager who obtains possession of a female under eighteen.
essential_elements: Buying, hiring, or otherwise obtaining possession of a child.
Intent, or knowledge of likelihood, that the child will at any age be employed or used for prostitution, illicit intercourse, or any unlawful and immoral purpose.
Punishment: imprisonment of either description, minimum seven years, up to fourteen years, plus fine.
Explanation 1's reverse presumption applies where a prostitute or brothel-keeper/manager obtains possession of a female under eighteen.
breakdown.how_to_read: Sections 98 and 99 form the supply-and-demand pair of the child-trafficking-for-prostitution scheme — note that the 'buying' side (Section 99) is punished more severely (mandatory seven-to-fourteen years) than the 'selling' side (Section 98, up to ten years with no mandatory minimum).
